#2557. Did Chiefs get hosed by NFL clock controversy? Breaking down the final seconds of Bills' wild Thanksgiving win

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL gave us a wild day of football on Thanksgiving, and the action didn't end until late Thursday night when the Bills' kicker Tyler Bass hit a 57-yard field goal on the final play to beat the Chiefs 13-10. Although the Bills got the win, it appears they may have gotten some help from the clock operator, who might have given Buffalo a few extra seconds at the end of the game.

After a punt by Buffalo, the Chiefs had a first-and-10 from their own 11-yard line with just 26 seconds left to play. The Chiefs couldn't simply kneel the ball and take the game to overtime because the Bills had all three timeouts, so Kansas City had to try to put together a drive.

On first down, Patrick Mahomes fumbled the shotgun snap, and that's where things started to get interesting with the clock.

After Mahomes fell on the ball, the Bills called a timeout, and the clock stopped at 19 seconds. However, before the Chiefs ran their next play, six seconds were added to the game clock, bringing it to 25 seconds. This means that the first-down play only took one second.

I am at a loss for words as how this first play only took *one* second off the game clock.Chiefs could have handled the ensuing sequence and punt differently and Buffalo potentially does not end up with enough time for the field goal attempt. pic.twitter.com/ILkv8LEXR7

The clip above was shared by Super Bowl-winning analytics consultant Ryan Paganetti, who used to make a living helping teams handle late-game situations like this. He was one of many people who were stunned that only one second came off the clock.

On the play, the whistle blew with 24 seconds left, and if you factor in that Bills head coach Joe Brady had to call a timeout, it seems like at least three seconds should have run off the clock.

On the next play, Emmett Johnson ran for a five-yard gain on second down. This play started with 25 seconds left on the clock and ended when the refs blew the whistle at 19 seconds. However, the officials added one more second to the clock, moving it to 20 before the start of the next play.

On third down, Mahomes threw an incompletion to Travis Kelce, which left just 15 seconds to play. At that point, it was total chaos: The Chiefs had to punt, and the Bills tipped the punt, making it more returnable for Greg Dortch, who took it 17 yards to Kansas City's 39-yard line. Dortch was tackled with four seconds left, which was just enough time for Bass to hit his game-winning field goal.

This final sequence is pure cinema. pic.twitter.com/jO4Fd8IOgu

The Bills definitely seemed to benefit from extra time here, but it's hard to say exactly how much. By my count, they got an extra three seconds, and in that case, Bass still would have been able to attempt the game-winning field goal with one second left. Other NFL reporters thought the Bills got even more time, with some believing Buffalo got anywhere from four to seven extra seconds.

If the Bills did get four to seven extra seconds, that would have created an interesting situation to end regulation. Matt Araiza's final punt would have come with just eight to 11 seconds left instead of 15.  In that situation, instead of returning the kick, Dortch could have called for a fair catch, and that would have set up a possible fair-catch free kick to win the game (this can be attempted even if the clock hits zero seconds on the play). The Chiefs also could have punted it out of bounds, or they could have had Araiza hit it low to ensure the ball would bounce so there would be no fair catch, but in either of those situations, the clock likely wouldn't have run out, and Buffalo still would have had time for one more play.

In the end, it does seem like the Bills got the benefit of a few extra seconds, but it's impossible to say whether that cost the Chiefs the game. Kansas City also had another controversy in the fourth quarter, when Rashee Rice made a catch for a first down on third-and-10 that was eventually overturned. Rice says he caught the ball, but the officials felt otherwise.

Although some NFL fans seem to think the Chiefs get every call, this game proves that not everything goes their way.

#2556. Grading the stress levels for 76ers, Celtics, Warriors and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Blake Griffin told an interesting story recently, recalling playing golf with former teammate JJ Redick. At that point, Redick was already retired and Griffin was nearing the end of his career.

This was before Redick became the head coach of the Lakers. He had some perspective on his post-playing days that he offered to Griffin, something that stuck with the longtime Clipper years later. Redick told Griffin that he wouldn't be "truly happy" until he retired. Knowing how that might sound, Griffin was quick to clarify that they weren't miserable playing basketball, but rather that the two men were similar in their extensive, obsessive preparation.

"The way I took it and the way I think that he meant it," Griffin told GQ, "is it's such a grind, mental grind, physical grind of putting literally everything you have into this thing. And then when you're done, you just find this new sense of peace."

Put another way, pressure is baked into being in the NBA. The severity might vary from player to player or team to team, but it's natural enough to feel a certain amount of weight given the intensity of the competition. With that in mind, here are some estimations on current stress levels around the league.

All things considered, the Sixers have to be pretty happy with how they've started the season. Even after the Blazers snapped their five-game win streak on Monday, Philly is 14-4 and sits atop the East. LeBron James, unsurprisingly, has been a fantastic addition, particularly as a distributor and playmaker. Jaylen Brown is playing his usual heavy minutes while shooting nearly 50% from the floor. And, crucially, Joel Embiid — who missed a combined 150 games over the previous three seasons — has appeared in all but four games to date. Those are all wins for the Sixers.

To the extent that there's any cause for concern here, it's how sustainable all this is for them. Of the 18 games they've played, they're a perfect 12-0 in the clutch (games decided by five points or fewer with five minutes or less to go). That's tops in the NBA, and they must feel good about being at their best when things get a little dicey. But as Tyrese Maxey pointed out earlier in the season when they were starting to fall into this rhythm of playing close game after close game, he and the Sixers would prefer to stack a few victories that don't cause them to sweat right until the end.

Winning in the clutch sure beats the alternative. For now, it's less of a problem than something to monitor.

Just a couple of weeks ago, the Celtics won the battle of frenemies and were perched atop the Eastern Conference. Things haven't gone quite to plan since then. All of a sudden, the Celtics have lost four in a row, including two one-point losses at Sacramento and Golden State. Boston handed the Kings just their second win of the season, and dropped the game to the Stephen Curry-less Warriors. Not the kind of basketball the Celtics are accustomed to playing.

Things haven't been easy lately for Boston. The Sacramento and Golden State games were on a back-to-back as part of a difficult, still-in-progress stretch in the schedule in which Boston plays six of seven on the road, culminating in another back-to-back when the Celtics face the Spurs in San Antonio this coming Sunday, followed by the Mavericks in Dallas on Monday.

Perhaps most troubling of all, two-way star Derrick White has been merely a one-way contributor for a while now. White had a disappointing shooting season a year ago. Considering his talent, the smart bet was that he would bounce back and be more efficient this season. That hasn't happened. White is shooting 41% from the floor and an abysmal 28.9% from deep. The 3-point mark is the worst of his career by a good stretch. He made just 2 of 12 from distance against the Warriors and was visibly frustrated with himself.

The Celtics have long had a theory of how they like to play: take and make more 3s than the opposition on any given night. When their shots are falling, they're tough to beat. When they aren't, anyone can knock them off. Right now, they're struggling, White in particular. Boston doesn't really have any choice but to let White try to shoot his way back into form. He's too important to their overall plans, and they'd never be able to replace his impact at the other end of the floor, where he remains one of the best all-around defenders in the league. Either he fixes his shot and Boston is back in business, or he doesn't and life at the office gets a lot tougher for everyone.

When the Timberwolves announced in October that Anthony Edwards would undergo an arthroscopic procedure on his right knee, it took some people by surprise. Edwards looked good to start the season. He torched the Heat in the opening outing, going for 45 points and draining nine 3s. In his fourth game, on the second night of a back-to-back, he put up 47 points in a close two-point loss at Cleveland — and then suddenly and without warning, he was out of commission and expected to miss approximately two months.

Edwards recently said that he "never wanted to have surgery" and he felt pretty good during the offseason. He thought he was managing the knee well then, and it wasn't swollen during the summer. But after the aforementioned back-to-back, the knee "was really bad, like painful to fly. So I'm like, 'I'm gonna get [the surgery].'"

Without him, the Wolves have fared better than some might have expected, going a tidy 10-4. They're third in the Western Conference, trailing only the Spurs and Lakers. That should have head coach Chris Finch and the Wolves optimistic about staying afloat until Edwards returns. Except no one seems to be sure when that might be, including Edwards, who recently cast some doubt on the initial timetable when he said he has "no clue" when he'll be back on the floor.

If we go by the original estimation, two months would put Ant in late December. Now that ballpark appears far less than certain. The Wolves have performed admirably with him sidelined, but in a loaded West, Minnesota will need Edwards back sooner than "no clue" if it wants to stay near the top of the conference and especially if the Wolves hope to make a deep postseason run.

Ant is the unquestionable leader in all departments for Minnesota. In his absence, things have sometimes felt a little tense  — to the point where one noted knucklehead has periodically gotten frustrated by another. Getting Edwards back would definitely help on the court. It wouldn't hurt the vibes, either.

What are the Cavs even doing? They're 9-9 after losing to the Bulls (without Caleb Wilson, no less) on Monday. That puts them one game up on the Magic for seventh in the East. They're just 2-6 outside of Cleveland. But hey, James Harden recently went for 51 points against the Pacers and now has more 50-point games in his career than Kobe Bryant. Maybe that will console Cavs fans. Seems unlikely, though.

When you reach the conference finals, bring back your four most important players and add a fifth starter coming off a promising season, the expectations are understandably high. So far, the Cavs haven't exactly met them. Cleveland has been a top 10 offensive team, but bottom 10 in defense. That leaves them pretty much looking like what their record indicates — average at best, a team that could lose to an inferior opponent (like, say, Chicago) on any random night in November.

It certainly hasn't helped that they've been without Evan Mobley of late. He's missed the last six games with a toe injury. Peyton Watson, the aforementioned addition to the starting lineup, hasn't been anywhere near as good in Cleveland as he was in Denver last season. All of that has left Donovan Mitchell with too much heavy lifting, and so far he hasn't been able to shoulder the load on his own. The longer this mediocrity continues, the more we're left to wonder whether the Cavs are overdue to shake up their starting unit and offload one of the big names.

[Looks around to see if anyone else is cringing] They just lost to the Pacers.

In fairness, no team has been hit with more major injuries than the Thunder. Jalen Williams (leg) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) could very well miss the remainder of the season after both underwent surgery, while Chet Holmgren (knee) is expected to miss at least three months. That's three of the team's five starters to begin the season. Not good. Except to hear the reigning back-to-back MVP tell it, there's something unexpected to be gleaned from the experience.

"Honestly speaking, it's kind of fun," Shai Gilgeous-Alexander said last week. "We've kind of had the wind at our back the last couple of years and had our way a lot of nights, and to have that kind of adversity, it's kind of fun. I embrace it. It'll make me better."

SGA has a different definition of fun than most people. After losing in Indiana on Monday, the Thunder are just two games over .500, which puts them 10th in the West. [Go ahead and cringe if you weren't already doing so.]

If there's any team that can withstand SGA's bizarre version of a good time, it's the Thunder. Sam Presti assembled the deepest team in the NBA, but there are limits to what even they can handle. In the absence of several key players, Ajay Mitchell, Jared McCain, Isaiah Hartenstein and others have all been tasked with picking up considerable slack. That includes rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz. When you're missing so many important pieces, you stop being deep at some point and just do your best to plug holes. Even the mighty Thunder can only do so much.

The Warriors snapped a five-game losing streak by beating the Celtics at home on Sunday in a white-knuckled one-point win. Alas, they only managed 88 points in the victory and the offense looked super sluggish yet again. Even with the win over Boston, the Warriors are 9-8 and 11th in the West standings. Things have gone sideways when you're looking up at everyone but the Pelicans, Clippers, Jazz and Kings.

The Warriors' start to the season was fun while it lasted. Yaxel Lendeborg played great — and talked just as well — and immediately cemented himself in the starting lineup, not to mention the Rookie of the Year race. Even more encouraging, Stephen Curry looked like a vintage version of himself again after playing just 43 games a season ago. Through the first 11 games this year, Curry was second in the league in scoring behind only Luka Dončić. He appeared sharp and healthy — until he came out of the game in Houston in early November while holding his side after playing just six minutes. Turned out to be an abdominal tear. The Warriors announced that he would be reevaluated in two weeks, though the general ballpark for that kind of injury is closer to a month.

Not great, especially considering the Warriors were hardly at full strength as it was. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody have yet to play a single minute while both recover from knee injuries. Meanwhile, Kristaps Porziņģis — who signed a new two-year deal worth $40 million in the offseason — is dealing with health issues and recently stepped away from basketball. Curry is the most critical piece of all, but not having several key components has left the Warriors painfully thin. That has reminded the Warriors how much tougher life is for all of them when Curry isn't on the floor and a rookie is suddenly tasked with leading the way.

The recently ended losing streak included a stretch at San Antonio, New Orleans, Dallas and Memphis during which the average margin of defeat was more than 27 points. The loss to the Spurs was bad enough that Lendeborg came back with a new cut, prompting Steve Kerr to quip that the rookie dealt with the defeat by "[chopping] all his hair off."

Through it all, Draymond hasn't been able to stop being Draymond. Green spent the run-up to the Celtics meeting warring with an NBA unc online, then got called for a tech while sitting on the bench during the game. Take a breath and go for a walk, man.

Curry can't return soon enough. If this goes on much longer, Yaxel and the rest of them will be fully bald.

#2554. Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

In possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

#2553. Broncos at Steelers: Why the NFL isn't allowed to schedule the Black Friday game for primetime

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the fourth straight year, the NFL is holding a Black Friday game, and for the fourth straight year, it will kick off at 3 p.m. ET, which makes it the most bizarre game on the NFL schedule. It's the only regular-season game all year that kicks off at 3 p.m.

With the Broncos and Steelers heading into a huge matchup, the NFL would probably prefer to put the Black Friday game in primetime — especially with all the Aaron Rodgers' drama surrounding the game — but the league can't do that thanks to a 65-year-old law.

Under the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, the league isn't allowed to televise any games on Friday or Saturday from the second weekend in September through the second weekend in December. Instead, those two days have been earmarked for high school and college football. However, there is a loophole in this rule: the NFL is ALLOWED to schedule a Friday game as long as it ends before 6 p.m. local time, which is how the league settled on a 3 p.m. ET kickoff time. It's basically the latest the game could start without running afoul of the SBA.

The NFL has generally avoided this issue by just not scheduling any Friday games. Since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, the league has only played a total of 16 Friday games and six of those have essentially been holiday games that were either played on Christmas Eve, Christmas or New Year's Eve. Those three holidays come AFTER the second weekend in December, so the NFL is allowed to put those games in primetime. For Black Friday, the game has to be in the afternoon.

The Black Friday game has worked out so well for the NFL that the league is actually kicking around the idea of adding a second game to the day. If that happened, it would likely be a doubleheader, with the first game kicking off at 12 p.m. ET and the second at 3 p.m. ET. Roger Goodell floated the doubleheader idea earlier this year, and although it didn't happen, it could still certainly be something we see on the schedule next year.

#2552. Padres add World Series standout reliever JoJo Romero as San Diego bulks up bullpen again, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The San Diego Padres have agreed to terms with veteran left-handed reliever JoJo Romero on a free-agent contract, ESPN reports. It's a three-year deal worth $21 million, according to The Athletic.

Romero, who'll be going into his age-30 campaign in 2027, is coming off a solid 2026 campaign for the St. Louis Cardinals and, after the trade deadline, the Milwaukee Brewers.

Those numbers don't include Romero's work in the postseason during the Brewers' run to the World Series title. In 8 playoff innings for Milwaukee, Romero pitched to a 1.13 ERA with 11 strikeouts against only one walk.

Earlier in the offseason, CBS Sports ranked Romero as the No. 31 free agent in the 2026-27 class. Here's part of that write-up:

"An appendectomy split Romero's season in two. He was great during the Brewers' postseason run and has been one of the game's better lefty relievers for four years now. His sinker/sweeper attack is plenty good enough that Romero does not have to be sheltered against righties."

For his career, Romero has a 3.51 ERA/119 ERA+ with a K/BB ratio of 3.86 across parts of seven MLB seasons. Over the last three seasons, Romero has a 2.91 ERA, which comes to an ERA+ of 140. He served as closer for the Cardinals for part of the 2025 season, which means he has late-inning experience. Across his 252 career relief appearances, Romero has limited left-handed batters to a slash line of .202/.281/.301.

Last season, the Padres returned to the playoffs in large measure because of their dominating bullpen. However, their most crucial setup man, lefty Adrian Morejon, is presently a free agent and thus may be bound elsewhere this offseason. Romero is no Morejon, but he does profile as a useful bullpen presence, especially if the gains he enjoyed while on the Brewers' watch prove to be sustainable.

#2551. NBA Hater Report: Celtics can't shoot, neither can Trae Young and James Harden isn't close to a top 10 player

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly. If you're not a fellow pessimist, proceed with caution.

The Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors. They failed to hit 100 points against the Kings and their 28th-ranked defense. They managed just 87 at Golden State.

Lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league). Only 25.6% of their shots are at the rim, the fourth-fewest in the league per Cleaning the Glass, and no team takes fewer shots per game from inside the restricted area.

They are about as extreme a jump-shooting team as you will find, and right now the shots are not going in. Over these last four, the Celtics have made just 28% of their 3s and 38% of their overall shots. Throw in 65% from the free-throw line and those are all bottom-two marks over that span, plus the 389 points they scored is the lowest over any four-game stretch since 2012 for a Boston offense.

It's not just the number of 3s the Celtics rely, sometimes more than others, it's the kinds of 3s. Every team wants the shots off ball and player movement, drives and kicks, drawing two and swinging, but when the Celtics aren't able to create the initial leverage by attacking the rim (they don't have to do this with just drives; they aim to do so by cutting and rolling, too), they end up taking more pull-up 3s than any team in the league, both as a total number and percentage of their overall shot diet.

Those are traditionally tougher shots, and indeed Boston is making them at a 33.5% clip. The Celtics also don't generate a ton of the coveted corner 3s (which are often a result of rim pressure) relative to their volume, and thus take more above-the-break 3s than any team. There are also a lot of one-on-one 3s; only the Lakers and Timberwolves take more 3s after three or more dribbles, and the Celtics make those at only 29%.

Bottom line, Derrick White is shooting 28% from 3 for the year and has missed 22 of his last 25 from deep (he had so many premium looks against Golden State and they just will not go in for him). Payton Pritchard has missed 21 of his last 29 from deep. Jayson Tatum is having a stellar all-around season and is leveraging his scoring attention to find teammates more effectively than ever, but quietly his shooting is in the dumps, too.

Tatum is shooting 42.6% overall and 33.6% from 3, both of which would be career lows if you discard the 15 games he played last season after returning ahead of schedule from the Achilles tear. Tatum has never been a particularly adept pull-up 3-point shooter, for which he'll probably always be prone to settling to at least some degree. Tatum's pull-up 3s over his last four full seasons:

Any team that launches as many 3s as the Celtics is going to endure some extreme ebbs and flows, and coach Joe Mazzulla remains committed to the course. "... If we're getting good shots, which more times than not we are, you have to be able to trust over the course of a season that that's going to work out," he said.

The truth is, the Celtics don't really have a choice other than to trust the shots to go in. They don't have a plan B to speak of. They don't get to the rim and they don't have a post presence. They have a gang of good shooters, but that doesn't guarantee good shooting.

The Celtics rely on getting more shots than their opponents by winning the turnover and offensive-rebounding battles, which they generally do, but as Mazzulla also said, "at some point you have to knock [the shots] down. That's just not happening right now."

After Harden scored 51 against the Pacers last Friday, Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson did the increasingly cliché "we've got to appreciate this guy" dance while calling Harden a "top 10 of all-time" player.

Kenny Atkinson after James Harden's 51-point game: "We've got to appreciate this guy. This guy is top 10 of all-time." pic.twitter.com/YUt2Y6pQYL

Remember, Atkinson is the guy who told reporters: "Analytically … we've won two out of three" right before the Cavaliers got swept by the Knicks in last year's Eastern Conference Finals. That was kind of overblown, to be fair. He was simply citing the types of shots the Cavs got vs. the ones the Knicks got, and that getting the right shots is a recipe for success more often than not, which every coach from the beginning of time has believed.

Atkinson just would've been better off if he'd gone the "make or miss league" route. Once you start invoking analytical results over actual results, you're going to get rightfully roasted as the number nerd that you are.

Through this lens, it makes sense that Atkinson thinks Harden is a top 10 all-time player. Numbers-wise, he's ninth all-time with almost 30,000 career points. He's 11th in assists and, barring injury, will almost surely pass Isiah Thomas for 10th by the end of the season. Only Stephen Curry has made more 3-pointers than Harden, who's piled up so many numbers he's actually top 20 all-time in steals.

Of course this is subjective, but this is my Hater Report, so allow me to hate. Harden was a manipulating machine of egregious proportions. I'm not saying he wasn't a great scorer, or even that he sometimes still isn't. Two things can indeed be true. But if we're going to start throwing around top 10, we're sure as hell going to factor heavily the conditions under which you dominated.

Harden played in the NBA's version of the steroid era. It was juiced up on some level for every scorer, but nobody mastered the dark arts like Harden, who cheated his way to so many phony fouls that guys were literally starting to guard him with their hands behind their backs.

Now listen, before you start with the "he wasn't breaking any rules" nonsense, keep in mind that steroids weren't technically illegal in baseball when Barry Bonds' head looked like it was going to pop. Harden scammed his way to more points than anyone in history. The flops and flails were impossible to stomach or, more importantly, defend against. Falling down on damn near every 3-pointer he took actually became part of his follow-through. I would only be mildly surprised if you hid a camera in his private workouts if he wasn't falling down in an empty gym, because he was so used to doing it.

This created more than just a gazillion free throws; it created a scoring environment in which Harden could operate against defenders who were way more frightened of fouling than being scored on. It was as if he was being perpetually defended by guys with five fouls.

Now account for the one-man-show usage. I remember Raja Bell once telling me there are way more players than you think who could score 25 points per game if given the opportunity. Hell, Darius Acuff Jr. is doing it right now and until a week ago, he was a teenager.

That's not to say anyone could do what Harden did, but given his set of circumstances, it's irresponsible to call him one of the 10 greatest players ever on numbers alone. Back in 2022, ESPN ranked him 50th all time, which feels much closer to reality, and he's only gotten worse since then.

I mean, just start rattling names off the top of your head. Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant, Wilt Chamberlain, Larry Bird, Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Hakeem Olajuwon, Kobe Bryant, Tim Duncan, Shaquille O'Neal. We're already at 12 and there's not even a debate with any of them.

No coach in his right mind would take Harden over Nikola Jokić, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Kevin Garnett, Karl Malone, Scottie Pippen, Charles Barkley, Isiah Thomas, Dwyane Wade or prime Chris Paul. I never watched Oscar Robertson, Jerry West, Julius Erving, Moses Malone, Elgin Baylor or some guy named Bill Russell, but something tells me the vast majority of coaches are taking those guys over Harden, too.

It bears repeating that none of this means to suggest Harden hasn't been an all-time player. He's a first-ballot Hall of Famer. He's not an empty-stats guy by any stretch; he led a team that very possibly would've won the championship in the middle of Golden State's dynasty were it not for a Chris Paul injury. But there are levels to this, and trying to elevate Harden into the top one on the strength of gaudy numbers in an absolutely juiced-up era of his game would be like trying to call Sammy Sosa one of the greatest hitters ever. It's just not even close to true.

Back in 2021, I called Young an average shooter who thinks he's Stephen Curry and got absolutely roasted for it. Turns out, I wasn't harsh enough on Young, whose shooting has been consistently deteriorating to the point that he is now a flat-out bad shooter. Even with a 7-for-15 run from 3 over his last two games, which at this point is a downright nuclear stretch for him, Young is shooting 32.5% from 3 and a pitiful 36.4% overall.

The fact that he's among the league leaders in assists means almost nothing; passing has always been his one elite gift (it goes largely hand in hand with his former ability to breach the paint at will), but it comes at the hefty cost of him controlling the ball for almost the same amount of time per possession as Luka Dončić this season. Just because those two were traded for one another doesn't mean they are, or ever have been, anywhere near the same caliber of player.

Even at his peak when he was one of the league's better shot generators, it was debatable whether you could justify sponsoring Young's personal dribbling show with your offense, let alone paying him max money given the defensive trade-off. But now that he can't shoot or beat anyone off the dribble, that $212 million deal the Wizards gifted him this summer, which was a disaster the moment the ink dried, somehow looks even worse.

Washington is trying to salvage some sort of value from Young. They're starting to take him off the ball some, which, given the good shooting the last few games, is going to give the apologists hope. Don't fall for it. The numbers, not just this year but going back a long time, speak for themselves.

There's a difference between a talented shooter and a good one. Young fooled people with range and confidence for a while, and he had an unearned marksman reputation that died hard. But the jig is up. This is an average shooter at best, and he's rarely at his best.

After losing four straight games by 20-plus while also being held under 100 points in each (an equation of futility that goes unmatched by any other team this century), the Warriors finally got their first win since losing Curry to an oblique tear by beating the aforementioned ice-cold Celtics.

It certainly wasn't because of their offense. The Warriors were once again held to double digits, managing just 88 points. Over this five-game stretch, the Warriors, who register a top-five offense with Curry, have scraped together an anemic 96.2 points per 100 possessions on 48.5% true-shooting, both being the worst marks in the league by a laughable margin.

Over this five-game stretch, the Warriors have been outscored by 108 points. The 1997-98 team that also lost four straight by at least 20 points was a minus-104 over that stretch. That was the season that Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo, mind you. The Warriors won 19 games. That's the kind of company these Warriors are trolling in right now.

If Curry doesn't get back soon, we might have to start worrying about Draymond Green putting Steve Kerr in a full nelson.

#2548. Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren

Tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX)

Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

On the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

The Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

The attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim showed some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The issue, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

The half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

Hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

In general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, showed excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He quickly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses

A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

Due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too quickly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

Overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

An additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant issues in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

By the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate new build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

Additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

Despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham showed general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

Through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game plan was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

In principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

The extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

The central issue with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

Both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

In general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

Sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

Towards the end of the half, Hoffenheim shifted its strategic focus from long balls to short build-up plays, which were mainly initiated on the right side. Kadeřábek positioned himself increasingly wide, which proved effective, as his direct opponent Son, starting from a half-space position, had to cover a long pressing distance and often arrived too late. This allowed Kadeřábek to receive the ball.

From there, Hoffenheim attempted to play quickly into depth to Hložek or Becker. However, Tottenham effectively defended this option through consistent man-marking. Becker’s dropping movements were frequently neutralized by Maddison’s covering shadow in the half-space, while Stach was largely covered by Richarlison, limiting the connections into the center significantly.

In the second half, Hoffenheim continued with this approach, but increasingly operated from a 2-3-4-1 formation, while Tottenham defended in a 4-1-4-1. The full-backs positioned themselves in extreme width early in the build-up phases to maximize the pressing distances of their direct opponents. This approach remained effective: With clean first touches, Hoffenheim occasionally managed to beat their opponents with dribbles.

The biggest difference from the first half lay in the subsequent movements from wide positions. Unlike in the first half, Hoffenheim refrained from structurally overloading the last line. The focus shifted towards deeper positioning to create diagonal passing options. This allowed Hoffenheim to either play directly behind Tottenham’s defensive line or use the space in between, where Hložek was frequently available for a pass.

There were also frequent rotations, for example between Bischof and Becker, which created additional dynamism. Kramaric often dropped into the defensive midfield space, allowing for the resolution of the isolation of that space by Richarlison, as Tottenham didn’t follow these wide runs in their man-marking system. This allowed Kramaric to distribute the ball on several occasions.

A positive aspect was that Akpoguma kept up with Kadeřábek’s wide movements, constantly offering a return pass option. Meanwhile, Stach often dropped deeper to cover space for counter-attacks—a lesson learned from the first half. Since Tottenham struggled to defend the width consistently, the pressing became deeper, and Hoffenheim’s pressure steadily increased.

Although Hoffenheim almost completely stopped playing long balls, the wide fullbacks presented themselves as viable options for diagonal switches, which were frequently sought. Sometimes Bischof also dropped wide to be available for these passes. These passes were mostly successful, as they were played into open spaces rather than into congested areas. Moreover, the 2-3-4-1 formation allowed for much better access to second balls due to the increased midfield presence.

For Tottenham, however, it remained a similar game to the first half. They still faced significant problems with the opponent behind them and technical difficulties in their ball retention play. Solanke added a bit more depth in the forward position, while Moore displayed more dribbling strength on the left wing. Despite some good individual actions, the problem areas—particularly in the final third from the very static 2-3-5—were still largely unresolved. Hoffenheim, on the other hand, simply had a better ball possession structure and dominated the game with nearly 61% possession. The counter-pressing issues ultimately led to Hoffenheim’s 1-2 goal.

Towards the end of the match, Ilzer switched to a 2-4-4 system with double-wide wingers, while Spurs also switched to a 4-1-4-1 formation, defending much wider. They tried to directly cut off the connection to the wide fullbacks, which they succeeded in doing effectively. Once they were bypassed, however, the fullbacks advanced well. The central players were now more tightly marked, following movements towards the ball. It wasn’t until Moore failed to notice Kadeřábek’s off-the-ball runs in the 88th minute that Hoffenheim managed to break free on the wing and score the 2-3 goal.

Overall, Tottenham’s initially wider setup made the half-space more accessible, which Hoffenheim repeatedly attempted to exploit. However, Moerstedt and Kramaric found few solutions against Tottenham’s well-defending center-backs. Several of these situations led to relieving counter-attacks for Tottenham, which were also the most dangerous for them in the second half. Especially towards the end of the match, as Solanke and Lankshear pressed for ball recoveries, Tottenham could quickly play vertically forward after regaining possession. Maddison’s dribbling pace was also frequently on display in these moments. It was clear that the fact Tottenham was ahead and Hoffenheim needed to win played into their hands.

The conclusion is ambivalent. Both teams are going through a difficult phase, which was reflected in the match—many fouls, turnovers, and long balls shaped the game. It was not a particularly convincing display from two teams that, in terms of personnel and concept, should be doing better. Both sides were often forced into wide areas or specific zones, which fragmented the combination play in the final third and lacked the necessary dynamism.

However, there were still glimpses of solid, familiar approaches, particularly from Hoffenheim, though the team still lacks the presence and stability required to compete against stronger opponents. As Ilzer highlighted in the post-match press conference: “We’ve learned that we need to be more stable to get the right results. In duels man against man, we lacked something. Still, you can see we can play really good football. We ruin a good game for ourselves when we make such simple mistakes. It was too easy for the opponent.”

Postecoglou’s team also showed deficiencies, especially in ball movement, presence in the final third, and intensity without the ball. Ultimately, the team that managed to relieve pressure better came out on top, while the other, had they played the second half like the first, might have seen a different outcome.

MX flirted with the RB school but secretly remained a romantic when it came to Guardiola’s football artistry. He is currently working as an analyst at a youth academy and is also an author for ‘spielverlagerung next generation.’

#2546. Dylan Larkin trade grades: Red Wings notch massive win in blockbuster NHL deal with Canadiens

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Detroit Red Wings have traded former captain Dylan Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a blockbuster trade, the teams announced on Sunday. This deal ends a bitter saga between Larkin and the Red Wings, and Montreal gave up a king's ransom to make it happen.

In addition to Larkin, Detroit sent a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Montreal. The Red Wings received forward Kirby Dach, goaltender Sam Montembeault, prospect Michael Hage, first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fourth-round pick.

Larkin requested a trade back in June, and his relationship with the Red Wings only grew more acrimonious with each passing day. As training camp opened in September, Detroit announced that Larkin had been stripped of his captaincy, and Larkin was booed by fans on opening night at Little Caesars Arena.

After recovering from an injury he suffered in camp, Larkin played 10 games before announcing that he would be sitting out in anticipation of the trade. While sitting out, Larkin racked up major fines, but his trade request has finally been granted.

When he's on the ice, there's no denying that Larkin can make a significant impact. The 30-year-old Larkin just notched 34 goals and 33 assists for the Red Wings last season -- his fifth straight year hitting the 30-goal mark -- and he was instrumental in Team USA ending its lengthy gold medal drought at the 2026 Olympics.

In his career, Larkin has totaled 278 goals and 371 assists in 818 games. The first game Larkin — a native of Waterford, Michigan — plays for the Habs will also be the first he's ever played for a team based outside the Wolverine State.

Larkin will give the Canadiens much-needed center depth, and he'll be under contract for a while. He's in the fourth year of an eight-year contract that pays him $8.7 million per season.

This trade fills a void that's existed in the Canadiens' lineup for several years now. Nick Suzuki has evolved into a legitimate star and a franchise-caliber No. 1 center. Beyond him, Montreal has struggled to find a true second-line center.

Larkin absolutely fits that bill. While he was a bit miscast in Detroit as a first-line center, Larkin is one of the best No. 2 options in the NHL, and he gives the Canadiens an elite one-two punch down the middle.

Did the Canadiens overpay a bit for a 30-year-old second-line center? In a vacuum, they did. However, taken in context, this deal makes plenty of sense for the Habs.

Montreal's championship window is just now opening. It already has an elite young core locked up for the next several seasons on team-friendly deals. Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Ivan Demidov, Juraj Slafkovsky, Lane Hutson and Noah Dobson are all 27 or younger and make less than $10 million per season.

That gives general manager Kent Hughes a bit more freedom to be aggressive on the trade market. Picks and prospects are nice, but they don't do much good for a team looking to make the jump to contender status in 2026-27. Besides, the Canadiens have been building their prospect pool for years now. It's time to flip some of those assets for proven star power.

The Canadiens paid a premium to acquire Larkin. There's no two ways about it. However, Montreal fills a major need and looks a lot more formidable in the Eastern Conference. The Stanley Cup window is officially wide open for the ascending Canadiens. Grade -- B+

Consider the situation interim general manager Shawn Horcoff faced. Everyone knew that Larkin wanted out of Detroit so badly that he was paying not to play for the Red Wings.

On top of that, Larkin had a full no-trade clause, and his list of approved teams amounted to no more than a dozen.

Should I also mention that Horcoff was thrust into this role in the midst of the offseason, when franchise legend Steve Yzerman was effectively fired for mishandling the Wings' rebuild?

Given all of that, it's hard to see this as anything less than a home run for Detroit. In fact, it's probably more like a grand slam. Not only did the Red Wings get multiple first-round picks and a couple useful NHL players out of the deal, but they also landed a legitimate blue-chip prospect in Hage.

The No. 21 pick in the 2024 NHL Draft, Hage is off to a roaring start at the University of Michigan this season with five goals and 21 assists in just 13 games. Detroit might have replaced one franchise center with another one, assuming Hage continues to develop at this rate.

This was a great piece of work from Horcoff, who probably just made a strong case for the full-time general manager gig in Detroit. This haul will allow the Wings to kickstart another retool or swing a big trade to bolster the current roster. Either way, the outlook just got a lot brighter in Hockeytown. Grade -- A+

#2543. MLB rumors: Kevin Gausman finds new home, plus latest on Royals, Phillies, Rockies, Cubs, Mariners, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hello, Thanksgiving Eve. This is generally not a day for a bevy of MLB moves, but with the CBA expiration right around the corner, there's been a flurry of moves this week. Perhaps that carries over for one more day until we get to Turkey Day? Buckle up.

Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.

The Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there. Sure enough, they are looking to add "at least two more guys that are no doubt rotation pieces," The Athletic reports. That could come via trade and/or free agency.

The Cubs rotation right now is Rogers, Justin Steele (returning from Tommy John surgery), Edward Cabrera (terrible in 2026), Javier Assad and, I guess, Braxton Garrett. Ben Brown and Cade Horton are recovering from major surgery and top prospect Jaxon Wiggins battled injuries and an exploding ERA in Triple-A last season.

The Cubs lost Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson, Clay Holmes, Shota Imanaga and Colin Rea to free agency, though all currently remain unsigned and any of them (Holmes is a great fit) could technically be brought back.

The Detroit Tigers have agreed to terms on a one-year, $25 million contract with veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman, ESPN reports.

Gausman, who turns 36 in January, is a reliable innings-eater who posted an ERA+ of 120 as recently as 2025. He's a two-time All-Star, and he's also finished in the top 10 of the Cy Young vote on three different occasions. This past season, the ERA was elevated relative to his usual standards, but at the same time he had an FIP of 3.74 and a K/BB ratio of 3.91. He'll slot in near the front of the Detroit rotation alongside Framber Valdez.

The Cleveland Guardians and 31-year-old lefty Foster Griffin have agreed to a three-year, $48 million contract, The Athletic reports. The Guardians acquired Griffin from the Washington Nationals at the 2026 trade deadline, and he was a part of the rotation from that point forward. Griffin inked a one-year deal with the Nats last offseason after rebuilding his repertoire and career across three seasons in Japan. In Cleveland, he'll rejoin a potentially impressive Cleveland rotation that also includes Gavin Williams, Parker Messick, Tanner Bibee, and Kris Bubic.

The Baltimore Orioles and outfielder Luis Robert Jr. have agreed to a one-year, $12 million contract, the New York Post reports. Robert Jr., 29, can still man center field, and he's coming off a 2026 season in which he produced at roughly the league-average level across 61 combined games for the New York Mets and Orioles. For his career, Robert Jr. has an OPS+ of 110 across parts of seven MLB seasons, and he earned an All-Star selection in 2023 with the Chicago White Sox.

The Colorado Rockies have overhauled their rotation, agreeing to a two-year, $32 million free agent contract with veteran left-hander David Peterson and a three-year, $42 million free agent contract with lefty Patrick Sandoval.

Peterson, 31, split his time this past season between the New York Mets and Chicago Cubs. Over his 148 ⅓ combined innings, he had an ERA of 4.79 and an FIP of 3.96. He enjoyed much better results after a deadline trade to the Cubs. Peterson earned his lone All-Star selection with the Mets in 2025.

Sandoval, meanwhile, struggled in his return from Tommy John surgery in 2026, putting up a 5.12 ERA over 70 ⅓ innings. The Rockies are banking on his return to form the farther he gets away from surgery.

Those two join Davis Martin and Luis Castillo (who has also worked out of the bullpen) in the revamped Colorado rotation as they try to find a way back to contention.

The Miami Marlins have agreed to terms with veteran catcher Gary Sánchez on a one-year, $6.5 million free-agent contract, ESPN reports. Sánchez, who soon turns 34, spent last season with the world-champion Milwaukee Brewers and served as William Contreras' productive backup.

Long a power threat, Sánchez, for his career, has averaged 34 home runs per 162 games played to go with an OPS+ of 107. In Miami, he'll serve as Joe Mack's backup

The Royals and free agent corner infielder Alec Bohm have agreed to a two-year, $20 million deal, reports The Athletic. He's coming off a rough year in which he hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with -0.2 WAR. He's gone as high as 20 home runs and 97 RBI in a season before, but he generally runs low-ish on-base percentages and scores negatively on defense.

The Royals have an opening at third base after trading away Maikel Garcia earlier this offseason, so it seems like Bohm will get a chance to start alongside all-world shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.

The top two free agent outfielders might be down to three suitors between the two of them. The Blue Jays, Phillies and Padres are in on Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, according to MLB Network.

There are obvious fits with either player on any of the three teams.

Arozarena, 31, is coming off his best all-around MLB season with 5.7 WAR. He hit .281/.381/.484 (148 OPS+) with 34 doubles, 26 home runs, 79 RBI, 26 steals and 113 runs.

Suzuki, 32, greatly improved his defense in 2026, leading to a career-high WAR of 5.1. He hit .270/.368/.473 (131 OPS+) with 26 homers and 86 RBI.

The Mariners have had meetings with four free agent relief pitchers, per the Seattle Times. Three of them are left-handers Alex Vesia and Gregory Soto and right-hander Bryan Abreu.

Abreu has been in the AL West for his whole career, having spent the entirety of his eight-year MLB career with the Astros. Last season, he had a 3.73 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 62 ⅔ innings, but walks have become a major issue. He issued 41 free passes. He's mostly been a primary setup man.

Vesia had a 2.64 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings for the Dodgers last season.

Soto posted a 3.63 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and 79 strikeouts in 67 innings. He has closing experience but has held several late-inning roles in his career.

The Brewers have re-signed right-handed relief pitcher Antonio Senzatela on a one-year deal worth a reported $4.75 million, the ballclub announced Wednesday.

Senzatela was long a starting pitcher for the Rockies, but converted to relief and was traded to the Brewers in front of the deadline last season. In 57 appearances in the regular season, he worked 73 ⅓ innings with a 4.05 ERA and 1.35 WHIP. He proved valuable in the playoffs, going 4 ⅓ scoreless innings.

Make sure not to misinterpret this report as the Diamondbacks actively shopping these guys, but "teams are checking on" D-backs starters Eduardo Rodríguez and Merrill Kelly, per The Athletic.

Kelly, 38, was 10-14 with a 4.94 ERA in 162 innings last season and has one year and $20 million left on his deal. Any inquiring team would be hoping for a bounceback season, as Kelly had a 3.47 ERA in his previous four seasons.

The 33-year-old Rodríguez might be a sell-high candidate here. There's one year and $19 million left on his contract and he's coming off his best season in a long time. He went 16-7 with a 2.89 ERA in 189 ⅔ innings.

Free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor has signed with the White Sox on a two-year, $17 million contract, according to MLB.com.

Taylor spent the last few months of last season in the same city with the Cubs and was excellent. In his 30 games on the North Side, he hit .351/.390/.500, spending time in all three outfield spots. Overall, he played in 97 games between the Mets and Cubs, posting 1.7 WAR as a fourth outfielder.

Taylor now joins Sam Antonacci, Braden Montgomery, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle and Tristan Peters in the White Sox outfield mix.

As the Mets continue to look for more pitching after the signing of Tarik Skubal, they are also "open to adding another outfielder as a bench bat," The Athletic reports.

The Mets' current outfield is Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge, with Nick Morabito as the bench option, though the latter may be ticketed for Triple-A to start the season should the Mets have their way.

The current Red Sox rotation is Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello. It's a quality fivesome, assuming everyone stays healthy. Therein lies the rub, of course, and you can never have too many starting pitchers. Sure enough, The Athletic reports that the Red Sox are seeking back-end rotation help. Among the listed options are Matthew Boyd, Robbie Ray and Hiromi Itoh, and any of those three would greatly bolster an already strong group.
