#2542. Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH

von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

On Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off. Nottingham, unbeaten in their last nine matches, has impressed this season with outstanding defensive work. Bournemouth, coached by Andoni Iraola and now unbeaten in 12 games, takes a completely different tactical approach compared to most other teams. In an interview with TNT Sports, Guardiola remarked: “Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton, and Liverpool play.” What exactly are these teams doing differently? Bournemouth’s approach will be analyzed in detail based on this match.

Bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao. Bielsa, widely known in the Premier League as the coach who led Leeds United to promotion, gained recognition for his style of play characterized by exceptionally high intensity in all phases of the game. According to Iraola, his own footballing philosophy has been significantly shaped by his former coach Bielsa.

In an interview with Sky, back when he was still managing Rayo Vallecano, Iraola stated: “I was very lucky to play for him (Bielsa) for two seasons as a player. I think he has another vision of football. They were two very good seasons for us, and, for me, it was a different knowledge.” He also explained: “I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him. I use a lot of things, especially with the ball. Offensively, his teams are very dynamic. He is willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder, offensively.”

Iraola’s tactical concept can be described as “organized chaos.” The aim is not to implement a positional system with perfect patterns of play. Instead, the focus is on creating problems for opposing teams by generating chaos. The idea is to force the opponent into unfamiliar, uncontrolled phases of play. A particularly important concept within this is highly intense, man-oriented, hybrid attacking pressing, designed to force the opponent into quick turnovers and a fast-paced, direct game.

„It is true that we like, and we perform better, in high-tempo games. We need to run a lot. We don’t need so much control, not in every single play, but I think we have the legs, we have the willingness, to go up and down.“ – Iraola

Accordingly, Iraola’s style of play could face challenges against deep-lying teams that deliberately thrive on minimal possession. These teams don’t need to engage with Bournemouth’s high-intensity game but can instead remain compact out of possession. They are not required to build up play from the back under Bournemouth’s pressing to maintain controlled possession but can focus on their own offensive transitions. This season, Nottingham has been one of the most successful teams in executing such an approach. Consequently, it was particularly intriguing to observe how Iraola’s Bournemouth would operate in possession against Nottingham’s deep block.

Iraola describes his philosophy in possession as follows:

“We have to prepare [positional] patterns, but we cannot just prioritise them. If you can see that you don’t have a teammate ahead, forget about the pattern, just drive the ball and try to force things to happen. I want him to attack first.”

Here lies the challenge I encountered while analyzing the game against Nottingham: how do you describe intentionally provoked chaos, where there are barely any fixed patterns? Only a few predefined sequences can be identified within the positional framework. The crucial question, therefore, is: what reference points structure Bournemouth’s possession play, and which principles of play create this chaos? Or, put simply: what “tools” does Iraola use in his style of play? To answer this, the positional framework of the game against Nottingham will first be examined.

Starting from a nominal 4-2-3-1 formation, Nottingham defended out of possession in a 4-4-1-1 or 4-5-1 structure. Nottingham focused primarily on defending and largely conceded possession to Bournemouth, a characteristic approach for the team. Under coach Simoes Espirito Santo, Nottingham has averaged just 40% possession this season.

Bournemouth, meanwhile, operated in possession with a positional 2-4-4 or 2-3-2-3 structure, featuring wide wingers and full-backs. From this setup, Bournemouth attempted to break through Nottingham’s deep block. On the (left) No. 10 position, Kluivert stood out with his exceptional dribbling ability and high agility. Central midfielder Christie alternated between the deeper right half-space as a right-sided No. 10 and the No. 6 position.

Nottingham was often forced back into their own half from an initially higher defensive pressing. When Nottingham attempted to press higher, Bournemouth’s center-backs positioned themselves wide, and goalkeeper Kepa moved up to form part of the back line. This made it nearly impossible for Nottingham’s lone striker to put significant pressure on the ball carrier. As a result, Nottingham dropped deep, retreated, and refrained from pressing the ball-carrying center-backs.

„I sometimes value much more a player carrying the ball and forcing things to happen. I think when you play too positional – one, two touches to find a free man – you sometimes lose the initiative from the players to just take their man on and attack the spaces.” – Iraola

This approach meant that Bournemouth’s center-backs were frequently required to dribble forward against stationary opponents, forcing defenders to commit. This often created 5v4 or 4v4 situations on the flanks, caused by the strong lateral movements of striker Ouattara and attacking midfielder Kluivert, combined with the forward dribbling of the center-backs. When no passingoptions were available, the team didn’t rebuild play, as is typical for positionally oriented teams. Instead, Bournemouth’s left center-back, Huijsen, was occasionally seen dribbling directly at the opponent’s last defensive line. It can be concluded that one of Iraola’s key principles of play is to attack vertically with the ball as early as possible.

Center-back Huijsen dribbles toward the final defensive line himself due to a lack of better-positioned deeper passing options.

The situations on the flanks during the center-back’s dribbling were played out in various ways. Sometimes the ball was passed to the wide player on the wing, who was tasked with taking on a 1v1 duel. This player was consistently supported by the full-back in a dual-width setup.

Particularly noteworthy were the positional rotations of the 3-4 players on the flanks. Full-backs, attacking midfielder Kluivert, striker Ouattara, and the winger frequently rotated out of their positions, occupying different spaces. What stood out was the consistent presence of a dynamic deep run within these rotations, forcing the opponent to cover the run and thereby creating space between their players.

The positional rotations with deep runs create passing options.

For example, the left-back Kerkez, during the center-back’s dribble, occasionally made deep runs into the half-space. Similarly, attacking midfielder Kluivert was often involved, sometimes shifting laterally to receive the ball and then driving forward at pace to attack the defensive block.

Nottingham responded to this from the 30th minute by attempting to apply more pressure on Bournemouth’s ball-carrying center-backs. The 4-4-1-1 shape was adjusted by removing the man-marking on defensive midfielder Adams. Instead, Nottingham transitioned into a 4-4-2 setup, aiming to position Adams in the cover shadow and step out earlier to press the center-backs. However, Bournemouth’s goalkeeper Kepa played so high in the back line that he was still able to connect with the now even wider-positioned center-backs, allowing them to continue dribbling forward.

The goalkeeper stepping into the back line creates a 4v2 situation, allowing the center-backs to dribble forward with less pressure from opponents.

“I would say they have the freedom to risk a little bit in the dribbles.“ – Iraola

Another key principle of Bournemouth’s possession game is diagonal, vertical dribbling. These serve as a chaos factor and are constantly utilized across all positions. As long as no teammate is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal, players are given the freedom to dribble. The skillful dribblers on the wings, the striker, and attacking midfielder Kluivert fit perfectly into this principle. The spaces opened up through the aforementioned rotations, particularly between the opposing players on the flanks, were mostly attacked through dribbling rather than passing.

The core idea behind this focus on dribbling is closely aligned with the concept of relationism. The goal is to make the team’s decisions less predictable for the opponent and to create a certain degree of chaos. Traditional positional play often limits players’ individual freedom, which reduces the element of surprise. However, Iraola’s execution of possession football differs significantly from relationism.

Instead of using a tighter structure to encourage combinations between players, rotations and larger distances between players are used to create spaces intended to be attacked through dribbling. It is crucial that these dribbles are always executed as vertical actions, continually putting the opponent under defensive pressure and thereby opening up other options.

Due to the larger spaces on the flanks, many dribbles are initiated on the wing, supported by the dual-width occupation of the winger and full-back. To enforce a successful follow-up action against deep-lying opponents, proper box occupation is a fundamental requirement. Iraola’s teams often flood the opponent’s penalty area with up to seven players, forcing the opposition right in front of their own goal. The goal is not necessarily to find the open player but to increase the likelihood of winning the ball after a cross in the penalty area. Second balls also play a significant role in this approach.

Risky dribbles have the additional advantage of provoking more frequent transition moments. When the opponent tries to transition offensively, they lose their compact defensive shape. Bournemouth’s flexible rest defense allows the ball to be immediately recovered after a loss of possession. Bournemouth’s rest defense typically consists of 3-4 players, depending on the attacking structure. In addition to the two center-backs, defensive midfielder Adams and the inverted, far-side full-back provide cover. If both full-backs or Adams are involved in the attack, Christie drops deeper to provide support and shifts closer to the ball.

On one hand, it’s important to highlight the excellent sense of positioning from the two central midfielders, Adams and Christie, in anticipating potential turnovers. Their ability to read these moments and their spatial awareness lead to many successful counter-pressing actions. On the other hand, the immediate pressure applied to the ball-carrying opponent after a turnover is notable, leaving the opposition with little opportunity to create controlled possession phases.

As a result, Nottingham’s offensive presence in the first half was minimal. Successful offensive transitions by Simoes Espirito Santo’s team were extremely rare.

The rest-defense structure in the 21st minute consists of the inverted Kerkez, the shifting defensive midfielder Adams, and the center-backs. At the same time, the ball-near teammates position themselves in response to the dribble in a way that allows them to immediately apply pressure if needed.

Another key principle of Bournemouth’s play is that after regaining possession, the first action is immediately directed forward. In contrast to traditionally positional teams, control is not sought through possession in chaotic situations but rather through constant transitions. The goal is to prevent the opponent from regaining their structure and settling into their usual rhythm. This creates intense pressure for Bournemouth’s opponents. As a result, Bournemouth often didn’t even need to break down Nottingham’s defensive block because the opponent never had the chance to regain their typical structure.

After recovering the ball, Bournemouth consistently looked to play forward into pressure. When positioned deeper (closer to their own goal), players in the forward zones immediately made runs into space to create vertical passing options. Even if the Bournemouth player who regained the ball was immediately under pressure, the first action was directed forward.

If necessary, a long ball was played toward the opponent’s defensive line, with a focus on winning second balls. This pressing game with an emphasis on second balls—often referred to as “kick and rush”—generated additional forced transition situations, preventing the opponent from finding their usual shape. The fact that four of Bournemouth’s five goals against the typically deep-lying Nottingham team came from deliberately provoked transition moments highlights the effectiveness of this approach.

In the second half, Nottingham switched to an attacking press in an attempt to create more scoring opportunities and overturn the 1-0 deficit. However, Nottingham was unable to pin Bournemouth in their own half as planned. Instead, Bournemouth played targeted long balls to one of their four advanced attackers or to the half-high positioned full-backs. Through a combination of winning second balls, dribbles, and central midfielders following up for lay-offs, Bournemouth was able to quickly progress into space and control the game from their own half. This led to Bournemouth scoring their second and third goals in quick succession. The final result was a resounding 5-0 victory for Iraola’s side.

So, what exactly causes the chaos in Bournemouth’s possession play? In summary, it is a combination of the principles discussed: playing vertically as early as possible; dribbling diagonally and vertically as long as no player is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal; and making the first action after regaining possession a forward one. The focus on vertical zones (reference point: opponent players) and second balls (reference point: the opponent’s goal) creates an intense and dynamic style of play that prevents the opponent from settling into their usual structure. Bournemouth is further aided by their attacking press, which was not analyzed in detail in this article but consistently provokes additional transition situations.

What can other teams take away from Bournemouth’s possession approach without abandoning their own philosophy? One lesson is the courage to consistently seek depth, provided the team has appropriate counter-pressing structures in place. Additionally, the dynamism of individual actions at Bournemouth is remarkable. Rarely have I seen such explosive runs into depth from other teams.

The final question is: what do the teams mentioned by Guardiola in the aforementioned interview have in common? All of them attack the depth quickly and frequently, making the game incredibly dynamic and intense. This forces the opponent to make decisions faster. After all, the main difference between good and very good players is the time it takes to make a good decision.

My recommendation is to watch games from 30 years ago. It quickly becomes apparent that football has become faster and more demanding.

“For me, the players are better than in 2003. They have to do the same things, but much faster. The physical demands are ridiculous. I doubt I could have played at this rhythm.” – Iraola

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

We fell for it again. Everyone underrated Houston. How could college basketball be so blind? Kelvin Sampson is as reliable as anyone in this sport and seems to own the nation's best team following the Cougars' run to the Players Era 8 title. Our Cameron Salerno projects that Houston will move up to No. 1 in the AP Top 25 rankings when they are released later today.

We also foresee Indiana moving into the top 25 for the first time in this young season thanks to a 2-0 week in which it beat No. 20 Arkansas and Kentucky. It also pointed the microscope on Mark Pope and his less-than-accurate explanation of his team's lack of experience.

Here is the tier in which we project the Hoosiers to land:

18. BYU (5-0) 19. Gonzaga (3-1) 20. Indiana (6-0) 21. Louisville (3-1) 22. Nebraska (6-0)

#2540. Why asking Trae Young to score less is a band-aid, not a fix for the Wizards' self-inflicted problem

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Washington Wizards entered Tuesday with a 7-11 record. In their seven wins, Trae Young is averaging just under 11.3 shot attempts per game. In those 11 losses, he's averaging 13.3. It's a small difference, but a notable one. The Wizards came into play Tuesday on a three-game winning streak, and a meaningful part of that streak has been Young spending less time on the ball.

In Washington's first 15 games, he averaged around 6.6 minutes of possession per game, tied for the third-most in the league. He's down to 4.5 in his last three games. He's dribbling around one fewer time per touch, and his average possession per touch is down around a second. These aren't glaring changes, but they've been helpful ones. It's not a coincidence, for example, that No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa's two best offensive games have come in this stretch.

Young, 28, has been a mess as a scorer this season. He's shooting just 36.4% from the floor and 32.5% on 3s. He's barely getting to the basket and struggling mightily when he's in the paint. He can't beat defenders nearly as easily off the dribble as he once could. Getting the ball out of his hands a bit more has been essential.

It's been an intentional shift on Washington's part. Wizards officials have asked Young to focus less on his own scoring and instead emphasize his playmaking, according to The Athletic. Washington certainly won't complain about a 24-to-7 assist-to-turnover ratio in that stretch. Young, despite his noticeable decline as a scorer, remains a stellar passer. That's typically how star decline works. It comes in bits and pieces. Even as essential components of a player's game degrade, years of accumulated basketball IQ allow him to continue finding ways to contribute. After years of abject tanking, the Wizards seemingly wanted an offensive organizer around to help give their younger players some structure. Young can still do that.

But we're in an increasingly financially unforgiving NBA, and the Wizards aren't paying Young a contributor's salary. They're paying him star money, and they chose to do so after just five relatively quiet games with him a season ago. His four-year, $212 million max contract will pay him at the top of the market through the end of Dybantsa's rookie deal. With Anthony Davis on the books through the end of Kyshawn George and Alex Sarr's rookie deals, the Wizards effectively traded the roster-building flexibility those cheap rookie deals afforded them for two declining stars.

Davis has justified the investment, at least as an asset. They haven't extended him. They could potentially flip him for more than they paid him. Young has not.

And that's the dilemma the Wizards are now in.

Clearly, less Young leads to more winning for the Wizards. But getting enough out of him to justify that enormous contract almost certainly requires more than they're currently getting. The entire value proposition of employing Young rests on him being a high-usage offensive engine. He just doesn't provide enough off-ball offensive value to justify what he gives up defensively at a max price point.

Take his shooting, for example. "Trae's got so much gravity," Wizards coach Brian Keefe told The Athletic. "When he plays off the ball, he's going to draw people, and then we're getting into actions with him on the second side that have been really good." There's something to this in theory, especially since gravity tends to rest more on reputation than reality. But Young has never been a consistently reliable catch-and-shoot player. He's averaging less than two catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game this season and has made around 28% of them. He's never averaged more than two catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game in a season.

Maybe he improves if his role demands more of these shots, but this is his ninth NBA season. That sort of shift this late in a career is rare.

It's a daunting change. Young spent most of his seven-and-a-half-year Atlanta Hawks run as almost entirely an on-ball player. He's never scored more than 39 points off of cuts in a single season. He has none this season. He's never been an especially active mover or screener, and even if he's grown on that front over the last few years, that's from a starting point of essentially zero. Asking Young to be less of a heliocentric shot creator is essentially asking Young to be a different player entirely.

That was the danger in paying Young sight unseen. They had no idea how he'd fit on this roster when they ponied up a max deal. If he'd picked up his player option and made this a prove-it season, they could have worked out the kinks and tried to sign him to a more appropriate deal next summer. The obvious argument here is that Young might have left had the Wizards refused to give him a long-term extension, but the counter here is that the Wizards would almost certainly have been better off if that had happened.

Stephen Noh's salary model estimates that Young is worth $26.3 million so far this season. That's a bit less than half of what he's getting. If that persists over the life of the deal, it's among the NBA's worst contracts. If his scoring continues to decline as he loses burst with age, it's a borderline crisis. Young may remain a passing genius, but passing skill is not a one-to-one match with passing value. It's easier to set teammates up when you're a dangerous enough scorer to consistently draw help. If Young isn't generating the same sort of advantages he once did, the passes that were once available to him suddenly become harder.

All of this puts the Wizards in an extremely precarious long-term position. They had to get the ball out of Young's hands more in the present. Too much of their offense involved players more important to the organization's long-term plans -- Dybantsa chief among them -- watching him dribble. A lower-usage Young probably makes the Wizards a better team simply by spreading usage to players who need more of it.

But that doesn't mean that a lower-usage Young is especially valuable. On-ball creation is where much of Young's value is generated. His scoring has declined so much that he's not generating the same value he used to, so all of this has stuck the Wizards between a rock and a hard place. They can try to maximize Young's skill set at the expense of everyone else, or they can try to maximize the team as a whole. But in doing so, they're not getting nearly enough out of a player they're paying to be a centerpiece. The latter is probably the right decision, but it's still a choice between two bad options. It's a band-aid on a self-inflicted wound.

#2539. What all 30 MLB teams have to be thankful for this year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Happy Thanksgiving, baseball enthusiasts! As the holiday name suggests, Thursday is a day to be grateful for the good things that have happened and the good things to come. Non-football sports are often secondary on Turkey Day, but baseball is a way of life as much as it is an interest. It's a companion, there with you every night during the summer.

On this Thanksgiving holiday, here is one thing fans of each MLB team can be thankful for this year. Mike Axisa handled the American League and Dayn Perry tackled the National League. Now sit back, loosen up your belt, and take a gander as you digest.

The Diamondbacks have been tantalizingly close to the playoffs the last two years. Know what might get them over the hump in 2027? The return of Corbin Burnes. Their on-paper ace returned from Tommy John surgery in time to make three subpar starts this past season, but his true comeback – one that brings with it the hope of a return to peak form – will come next season. Assuming all goes well, Burnes will be a huge boon to the Snakes' hopes in 2027.

On the field, 2026 went about as poorly as possible for the Athletics. Almost every core player missed significant time with injury and their pitching was wretched. At a time when the A's are supposed to be building up for their move to Las Vegas, they went from 76 wins in 2025 to 64 wins in 2026. Yeesh. The good news is the A's have new leadership. President of baseball operations Taylor Smith comes over from the Red Sox and general manager Cam Castro joins from the Brewers, which are two pretty good teams to emulate. The Athletics needed new voices and a fresh perspective in the front office, and they have it now.

For the Braves, their gratitude comes from reflection. Last season, they rebounded from the disappointments of 2025 to log 94 wins and claim the National League East title. As well, they won a postseason series for the first time since 2021. On top of that, the Braves exacted revenge upon their NL East rivals, the Phillies, by defeating them in the Wild Card Series. That comes after the Phillies eliminated the Braves in 2022 and 2023.

The Orioles again failed to reach the postseason this past season and they traded away Adley Rutschman, once the face of the franchise, at the deadline. It was a disappointing year through and through. Year 1 of the Pete Alonso experience certainly went well, though. He led all first basemen with 5.0 WAR, led the league with 43 home runs and 113 RBI, and finished fifth in the AL MVP voting. Right-handed power is in shockingly short supply these days and the O's have one of the very best right-handed power hitters in their game anchoring their lineup. Big money free agent signings should all work out as well as Alonso did in 2026.

There is a lot to like about the Red Sox at the major-league level. They've added Jake Bauers, Curtis Mead, and Adley Rutschman to their lineup in the last four months or so, and the rotation is stacked with Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suárez, and Payton Tolle. Boston also has one of the very best prospects in the game knocking on the door in Franklin Arias. The shortstop of the future (and, very soon, the present) slashed .323/.400/.557 with 25 home runs and only 74 strikeouts in 117 games between Double-A and Triple-A in 2027. Not-so-bold prediction: Arias will be the Red Sox's Opening Day shortstop next year.

The Cubs are very much in contending mode right now, even if their last two trips to the postseason haven't yielded anything close to the desired results. The foundation, though, is there, and it's Pete Crow-Armstrong. Not only is he one of the best all-around and most electric performers in the games, but he's also just 24 years of age. Best of all, at least from the Cubs' standpoint, he's under contract through 2032 at what will almost certainly turn out to be deep-bargain rates.

Here is the complete list of right-handed hitters to hit 30 home runs, walk 100 times, and strike out fewer than 130 times since the 2020 pandemic season: Miguel Vargas in 2026. That's it. The last righty hitters to do it before Vargas were Alex Bregman and Mike Trout in 2019. Munetaka Murakami may have gotten the headlines, but Vargas was the White Sox's best player this year. He's a legitimate star with a special blend of contact, power, and plate discipline. Getting Vargas for spare parts (Erick Fedde, Michael Kopech, Tommy Pham) at the 2025 trade deadline has proven to be a terrific move by POBO Chris Getz.

The Reds are a bit rudderless right now, but their rooters can be grateful that sparkling shortstop Elly De La Cruz is on the roster. With a 30-30 season and a breakout campaign with the bat freshly behind him, De La Cruz is poised to become an MVP candidate as a 25-year-old in 2027. Whether that's with Cincy long-term or as a blockbuster trade piece that nets the Reds a true haul remains to be determined.

It has never been a question of talent with Chase DeLauter. He had just been held back by injuries, most notably a series of foot injuries, dating back to his time at James Madison. This year, though, DeLauter stayed on the field and turned in an excellent rookie season: .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and only 82 strikeouts in 133 games. The underlying data (exit velocity, etc.) is impressive. Once DeLauter learns how to pull a few more balls in the air rather than push them the other way, he'll be a monster. The Guardians are in perpetual need of offense and DeLauter looks like a long-term keeper in the middle of the lineup.

Rare is the primary catcher who tops 40 home runs in a season, but that's exactly what Hunter Goodman did in 2026. That makes him a hugely valuable presence moving forward. Whether that's as a Rockie as the modernized front office gets them up to speed or as a blockbuster trade target for other teams is TBD. Either way, he's a needle-mover. For those curious, 25 of his 41 home runs last season came away from Coors Field.

It ultimately did not happen, but as late as August, Kevin McGonigle had a chance to finish with the third-highest WAR by a rookie position player in the Expansion Era (since 1961), behind only Mike Trout and Aaron Judge. Even without that admittedly obscure distinction, McGonigle was sensational in 2026, slashing .278/.376/.430 with 18 home runs and nearly as many walks (95) as strikeouts (100). He won American League Rookie of the Year and finished seventh in the AL MVP voting. Best of all, the Tigers wisely locked McGonigle up to an eight-year, $150 million extension in April. That will keep him in Detroit through 2034 and it already looks like a bargain.

I don't think there's a better or more imposing hitter in baseball than Yordan Alvarez. He's so big and scary! Years of near-MLB-best performance finally culminated in an AL MVP award this season as Air Yordan slashed .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and nearly as many walks (109) as strikeouts (120). Here's something that flew under the radar: Alvarez was intentionally walked 33 times, second most in American League history behind Aaron Judge's 36 in 2025. You know you're good when teams put you on intentionally that much. The Astros eked out an AL West title this past season and Alvarez was the single biggest reason.

Bobby Witt Jr. turned in another terrific season and finished second among all players with 7.0 WAR. He's a given here. Now he has a great running mate in Jac Caglianone, who reined in the swing-and-miss and slashed .289/.340/.494 with 23 home runs. His exit velocity and hard-hit data are among the very best in baseball. All Caglianone needs to do to become one of the game's truly elite hitters is reduce his ground ball rate, which was an elevated 46.3% in 2026. You'd like to see that number down around 38% (if not lower) for a guy with this much power. Point is, the Royals have a second building block in their lineup.

The Arte Moreno Reign of Error is over. Moreno has agreed to sell the Angels to Stan Kroenke for the tidy sum of $4 billion, and, if nothing else, it really can't get any worse. I mean, the Halos lost 100 games for the first time in franchise history in 2026. Kroenke's other franchises have all won a title recently (Arsenal F.C. in the English Premier League, the NBA's Denver Nuggets, the NHL's Colorado Avalanche, etc.) and tend to be smart, well-run organizations. It will take some time to turn the Angels around, but at least now there's some hope. Under Moreno, there wasn't.

The Dodgers have plenty of veteran star power on the roster, fronted of course by Shohei Ohtani. Now, though, they have some young upside on the way in outfielder Josue De Paula, who's one of the top prospects in all of baseball. The 21-year-old lefty batsman has star upside at the plate, and coming off a highly successful cuppa coffee in 2026, he's poised for a bigger role and maybe Rookie of the Year honors in 2027.

As the Marlins methodically work their way back toward relevance, Otto Lopez has emerged as A Dude. Over the last three seasons, the shortstop has increased his WAR from 2.8 in 2024 to 3.6 in 2025 to last season's mark of 6.1. Going into his age-28 season, Lopez is operating at peak and may be the most underrated player in baseball right now.

This one's not challenging. The Brewers are fresh off the first World Series title in franchise history, and those credentials are burnished by a 2026 regular season that saw them post the best record and best run differential in all of baseball. It's not "just" a championship; it's dominance en route to that championship. Fans of the Crew should thus be the most grateful of all right about now.

This month was pleasantly surprising and productive for the Twins. First, Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer, and I'm not sure anyone expected that. Getting him back on a one-year contract is a win even if it is a big salary. And second, Sonny Gray returned to Minnesota on a two-year deal worth $55 million (with an opt out). Just like that, the Twins welcomed back a key middle-of-the-order hitter and stalwart catcher, and upgraded their rotation significantly. This past season was a major disappointment, for sure, but I don't think you need to try all that hard to see this team contending for the AL Central title in 2027.

Mets fans, your team just signed far and away the top free agent on the market in ace and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. Yes, the cost was high, but the Mets now have at the front of the rotation perhaps the best pitcher in all of baseball. The pressure is on both team and player, but the pairing is made to order for a team that needed such a presence on the staff.

I'm partial to Ron Guidry's 1978, but the case can be made that Cam Schlittler just turned in the greatest pitching season in Yankees history once you adjust for era. His 215 ERA+ is in fact a franchise record for a qualified pitcher, besting Guidry's 208 ERA+ during that 1978 season. Regardless of where Schlittler's Cy Young campaign ranks historically, he emerged as a bona fide ace in his first full MLB season, one in which he proved himself to be a Red Sox killer (always a plus for a Yankee). The Yankees turned a seventh-round draft pick into a front-of-the-rotation starter. If you can't be thankful about that, what can you?

The Phillies are finally willing to move the defensively deficient Trea Turner off of shortstop. That's a welcome development. Speaking of welcome developments, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is reportedly willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phils. That would be a great targeted strike by Dave Dombrowski and help keep Philly's contending window open a bit longer. And even if not, at least they're trying.

Shortstop Konnor Griffin held his own as a 20-year-old rookie last season, putting up a 2.1 WAR in just 80 games. It's rare enough to even reach the majors at such an age, let alone provide value. Griffin looks like a regular All-Star selection and occasional MVP candidate for years and years to come, and the Pirates have secured his services through the 2034 season.

It's about the future in St. Louis. Under lead operator Chaim Bloom and the built-out player-development program, the Cardinals in short order have gone from a mediocre farm system to one of the very best in the game. Pair those incoming talents with in-place youngsters like JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker, and the future for the Cardinals is shimmering.

There's no replacing the late Peter Seidler, the beloved Padres owner who distinguished himself by caring about and committing to winning more than almost any other owner in the game. Now, though, new owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones have signaled they, too, have bold intentions with the Padres. They were seriously in the bidding for Tarik Skubal, and while they didn't land the top free agent, their presence in the fray suggests payroll retrenchment isn't on the way in San Diego. That's encouraging.

The Giants seem forever in need of offense lately, and rookie Bryce Eldridge in 2026 gave them value in the present and promise for the future. One of the top offensive prospects in baseball coming into 2026, he proved himself and then some after arriving in San Fran to put up a 133 OPS+ in 107 games. That was good for seventh place in the National League Rookie of the Year vote. He's looking like a middle-of-the-order presence for years to come, and that's just what this flagging organization needs.

Gosh, what a disappointing season for the Mariners. They went from Game 7 of the ALCS in 2025 -- five outs away from their first pennant! -- to 76 wins and failing to reach the postseason in the sad sack American League in 2026. Woof. On the bright side, Kade Anderson, the No. 3 pick in the 2025 Draft, quickly emerged as baseball's top pitching prospect and made seven solid big league starts late in the season. His minor-league performance was simply incredible: 1.06 ERA with 135 strikeouts and only 13 walks in 93 ⅓ Double-A innings. Anderson's emergence allowed the Mariners to trade Bryce Miller for Maikel Garcia, a trade I loved for Seattle.

Tobias Myers for Junior Caminero in November 2021 is already one of the most lopsided, landscape-altering trades of the generation, and Caminero has only played two full seasons. He hit 40-plus home runs in those two seasons, joining Hall of Famer Eddie Mathews as the only players in history to hit 40 homers twice before their age-23 season. Caminero is one of the very best hitters in the game and the Rays stole him away from the Guardians for a depth arm in Myers, who never threw a single pitch for Cleveland. A heist of seismic proportions.

If not for February UCL surgery, top prospect Sebastian Walcott likely would have made his MLB debut this summer. He returned to the field in mid-July and didn't miss a beat: .325/.401/.590 with 10 home runs in 41 minor-league games while reaching Triple-A. Walcott mashed in another 16 games in the Arizona Fall League as well. The UCL surgery was a tough break, but Walcott had a smooth recovery and will soon join a Rangers team that needs all the offensive help it can get after finishing 25th in runs in 2026.

I could go with something cheeky like "2026 is over (especially for Vladimir Guerrero Jr.)," but nah, we'll instead give Dylan Cease and Kazuma Okamoto their flowers for tremendous first seasons with the Blue Jays. Cease had the league's highest strikeout rate and finished second in the Cy Young voting in Year 1 of his seven-year, $210 million contract. Okamoto slugged 33 home runs and looked better at third base than I think even the Blue Jays expected. He signed a four-year, $60 million deal last offseason. A lot went wrong for Toronto this past season, but Cease and Okamoto went very, very right.

James Wood. There are many reasons for Nats partisans to be encouraged about the current direction of the organization and the young talent in place, and then there's Wood. Wood just recently turned 24, and he has a career OPS+ of 134 in more than 1,600 plate appearances at the highest level. If there's a candidate for "the National League's answer to Yordan Alvarez" right now, then it's Wood.

#2537. Inter Milan U19: Team Analysis – MH

von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

Inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

Inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

To build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

The primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

If only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be quickly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

To effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

Through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

Even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

This three-man buildup creates new passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

Due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

Additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

The follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

One of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

While striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

The pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

Another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

Depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

Once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

Especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

As the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

Inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

In possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2536. NBA rumors: Latest on Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns, plus Wizards' Anthony Davis plan, a Nets trade candidate

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We may be weeks away from the unofficial beginning of trade season on Dec. 15, but the NBA rumor mill has been surprisingly active. With a number of big names seemingly set for availability before February and a packed championship race, the next few transaction cycles figure to be loaded with movement. Let's dive into the latest batch of rumors

Karl-Anthony Towns had a tense set of contract negotiations with the New York Knicks last offseason, but if there was any fear that it would spill into his performance, those have quickly been squashed. Towns, frankly, has been New York's best player this season. He's the NBA's rebounding leader, has maintained his defensive improvement from last season and the uptick in his playmaking that came in the playoffs, and of course, he's averaging a very efficient 22 points per game or so for a defending champion that has won five games in a row.

Technically speaking, the Knicks could still extend Towns during the season. Multi-year contracts cannot be extended once the season has begun, but Towns could sign an extension by declining his $61 million player option for next year. However, there's little indication that the Knicks have changed their stance on wanting Towns to take a meaningful discount from his max on his next deal. "The Knicks, I think, would lose him if he opted out this summer and went into free agency," SNY's Ian Begley even said on "The Putback."

Now, we can qualify this as something closer to informed speculation than hard reporting. There is also plenty of time for things to change, either for the Knicks to offer more money or for circumstances to change in such a way that Towns would take less. If the Knicks win another championship, that certainly helps his case.

The point that Begley is making here is that Towns is almost certain to receive substantial interest in free agency this offseason, with plenty of teams likely eager to pay him after the start he's had. If the Knicks were willing to increase their offer to a suitable level, well, this could be done already. A number of notable teams led by the Golden State Warriors could create substantial cap space this offseason. If one or more of these teams is willing to offer Towns the full max and the Knicks aren't, then yes, New York would seemingly be in danger of losing its star big man.

Towns has reportedly been willing to sign for less than the max. There is simply a gulf between what he considers fair and what the Knicks have thus far been willing to offer. The Knicks drew a hard line in the sand about going above the second apron last offseason and it cost them backup center Mitchell Robinson. With new contracts for Jalen Brunson, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart also looming, the Knicks are pinching pennies even as the defending champion. There's still plenty of time for the two sides to find a middle ground here, but for now at least, it doesn't seem like Towns' strong start has changed much on New York's end.

There was a widespread assumption for a good chunk of the offseason that the Washington Wizards got Anthony Davis to flip him. He's 33. They didn't extend him when they had the chance in August. The drawn-out nature of LeBron James' free agency led plenty to believe he was trying to engineer a reunion with his former Los Angeles Lakers teammate. Alas, no deal came. When the Wizards started 4-11, the rumors picked back up.

And yet again, Washington's plans for Davis remain unclear. Reporting for The Stein Line, Jake Fischer noted that while several league cap strategists have told him they expect Davis to be traded, he has received pushback to the idea and does not believe, for now, that any trade is imminent. We are of course in peak posturing season. Plenty can change between now and February. Yet Washington already resisted trading Davis through one transaction cycle. A second doesn't seem out of the realm of possibility.

Davis is in the middle of a renaissance season. He's averaging over 25 points and nearly 10 rebounds a game for a floundering Wizards team with minimal spacing. Still, his age and injury-proneness make him an enormously risky extension bet. Even in the best-case scenarios, it's unlikely that he remains a star-level player by the time Washington's young prospects are ready to contend seriously. Besides, with Trae Young's disastrous max contract on the books, extending Davis risks depriving Washington of any financial flexibility for the next several years. Couple that with the decline in Alex Sarr's usage when he shares the floor with Davis and there's plenty of reasonable motivation for Washington to pursue a trade. The longer they wait, the more they risk an injury that saps his value.

The Wizards gave up two first-round picks to get Davis, but they were weak ones: No. 30 overall last season, and a top 20 protected pick that is mathematically unlikely to actually convey. For now, they should be more than capable of turning Davis into a net asset profit by getting real draft capital for him. Yet the longer they hold out, the more believable the notion of keeping him actually becomes. With nothing realistically on the table from a salary perspective until at least Dec. 15, this sort of messaging early on makes plenty of sense. Whether the Wizards ultimately do keep Davis in the long run remains to be seen.

From one player who has lasted longer with his current team than expected to another, Michael Porter Jr. was one of the more obvious trade candidates of the 2025-26 season. The Brooklyn Nets were tanking. He had a career year. Flipping him to a contender was the obvious move. But the Nets are notoriously patient when it comes to such trades. They held out longer than expected on Mikal Bridges and Cam Johnson and netted better packages for both than anyone could have imagined.

But they don't have that sort of time with Porter, who is in the last year of his contract and whose numbers have slipped back closer to their norms after last year's breakout. Unsurprisingly, he is a name that has featured heavily in the early season rumor mill, and the New York Post reported Tuesday that the expectation is that he is indeed moved. "Michael Porter is a pending unrestricted free agent. As one still unsigned to an extension, he's widely expected by league personnel to be dealt by the trade deadline," Brian Lewis wrote.

Porter, by virtue of his strong 3-point shooting, should be a relatively comfortable fit on most teams offensively. He was heavily linked to the Detroit Pistons last trade deadline, but no specific suitors have yet emerged as new destinations this year. His $40.8 million cap figure will be tricky to trade, but if he and a new possible team are on the same page about the basic framework of a long-term deal, that's not an insurmountable problem. The Nets traded for Julius Randle at power forward in the offseason and have a number of young shot-creators to develop. If they viewed Porter as a major part of their future, they could have used cap space to renegotiate and extend him last offseason. They didn't, and now he's an obvious trade candidate for February.

#2531. Connor Bedard injury: Blackhawks star's latest issue shines light on a stalled out rebuild in Chicago

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

An awful start for the Chicago Blackhawks only got worse on Monday night when the team announced that captain and superstar forward Connor Bedard would miss four months after undergoing right shoulder surgery.

On Nov. 17, Bedard injured his shoulder on a face-off and left the ice in a lot of discomfort. After deliberating whether to rehab the shoulder or get surgery to repair the issue, Bedard opted for the latter half. That will sideline him longer now, but it could provide a more permanent fix.

Bedard missed the first two weeks of the season while recovering from surgery on his left shoulder in the offseason. The Blackhawks captain suffered that injury during summer training -- and that also occurred on a seemingly innocuous play.

Even after Bedard's initial injury, Chicago hoped that the 2026-27 season would be a step in the right direction amid a lengthy rebuild. Instead, the team is on track to finish with fewer points this year than last year -- despite playing two more games.

The Blackhawks are 8-14-2, which is good for 30th place in the NHL. Only the aging Pittsburgh Penguins and actively tanking Vancouver Canucks sit below them. The prospects Chicago has drafted in recent years haven't shown adequate process at the NHL level, and they've got no veteran support around them.

With Bedard out for an extended period of time, the Blackhawks must re-assess their long-term vision.

When healthy, Bedard has shown that he can be a true superstar. The 21-year-old has 82 goals and 139 assists in 234 career games, and he began the 2025-26 season on a torrid pace before, well, suffering a shoulder injury.

And therein lies the biggest question about Bedard's future as a true force in the NHL. Is this just bad luck, or will his lack of durability prevent him from reaching the potential that's evident when the puck is on his stick? Chicago can only hope its the former, but this isn't the first time Bedard has missed significant time due to injury.

This is now Bedard's fourth NHL season, and he's played 70-plus games just once. That was in the 2024-25 season, when he played all 82 games and tallied 67 points.

Last season, a right shoulder injury forced him to miss 13 games and snuffed out his tremendous start. Months later, Bedard injured his left shoulder after taking a spill during summer workouts. That prompted one surgery, and his latest right shoulder injury prompted another procedure less than five months later.

I'm certainly not a doctor, but two shoulder surgeries that close together seems concerning, especially for how much the Blackhawks have invested in Bedard.

In 2022-23, the franchise completely demolished its roster in hopes of landing the No. 1 overall pick. It worked, and Chicago got to draft Bedard, the consensus top prospect in the class. This past summer, Bedard and the Hawks agreed to a five-year contract extension worth $75 million.

If Bedard gets healthy and plays anywhere near his peak, that will be a discount. If injuries continue to limit him, the Blackhawks will have a serious problem on their hands, but that probably goes without saying.

Even with Bedard in the mix, the Blackhawks' rebuild wasn't going particularly well. Chicago hasn't finished above .500 since the 2019-20 season, which was cut short due to the COVID-19 pandemic and was three years before they selected Bedard in the 2023 NHL Draft.

The upshot of all that stinking is that the Hawks stocked up on premium draft capital. With that, they've built what should and exciting young core for the franchise. Not including Bedard, Chicago has seven skaters who were selected in the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

Kantserov has shown scoring touch at the NHL level, Nazar has been inconsistent and flashed upside and Rinzel has started to show signs of progress on the back end. Other than that, none of those young guns are ready for primetime. That's not say they will never get there. In particular, Frondell and Levshunov have the tools to get there.

It's just that the results have been really ugly to this point. According to Natural Stat Trick, the Blackhawks rank 30th in expected goals share at 42.5%. The team's minus-32 goal differential ranks 31st in the NHL. To put it more succintly, Chicago is getting what it deserves more often than not.

With Bedard out for the next four months, it's time to see who can sink and who can swim. Stop playing 37-year-old Ian Cole almost 20 minutes per game and let defensive prospects see the ice more. Tyler Bertuzzi has been incredibly ineffective, and his contract is moveable. Trade him to a contender and open up another spot for a young player in the top six.

If the team doesn't make any progress over the last 60 games of the season, it may be time for a wholesale changes at the top. General manager Kyle Davidson was tasked with orchestrating a rebuild that's going nowhere quickly. Jeff Blashill is 37-53-16 behind the Blackhawks' bench, and he's 241-314-88 in his coaching career.

If Chicago continues to flail at the bottom of the standings, how much worse could it possibly get? A new set of eyes in the front office and a new voice in the locker room wouldn't be the worst ideas.

Philly made just nine of 33 on its 3-point attempts in Monday's loss. LeBron had 23 points, his most thus far as a Sixer. Over the last three, James is averaging 22.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 5.0 assists. Jaylen Brown returned from a two-game injury absence and had 20 points. Walker had 10 points and five boards in 20 minutes.

The 76ers are committing just 11.9 turnovers per game, fewest in the league. They have six wins this season when trailing at any point by double digits, most in the league. But the defense hasn't been great of late as Philly has not held an opponent to fewer than 110 points since Nov. 4 against the Pistons.

While Miami leads NBA Cup Group B at 2-0, Philadelphia is solo third at 1-1, so a loss here would likely mean the Sixers aren't advancing. They are +155 to do so and +180 to win the group, while Miami is the +115 group favorite and -115 to advance.

This marks the first meeting of the season between the teams after the Heat won two of three last year. Miami is 6-1 in the past seven meetings overall.

BetMGM rocks with its pre-made single-game parlays, so I'll just take the one on Philly and with Brown scoring at least 20. Maybe we get lucky and Giannis doesn't play ... or at least is limited.

The Sixers haven't lost back-to-back games yet. Brown is averaging 22.4 PPG this season and has scored at least 20 in three straight. The model has him with 22.8 tonight and Philly by five. Check out other expert picks in the SportsLine daily newsletter.

#2529. Black Friday bargains: Four MLB free agents who could provide the most bang for your buck

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Like us regular folks, MLB front offices love a discount. Trevor Megill, who recorded the last six outs of this year's World Series clincher, has been a tremendous bargain for the Brewers. They got him from the Twins for a player to be named later on April 23, 2023. Megill has since blossomed into an All-Star closer. Shrewd piece of business, that was.

So, on Black Friday, a blessed day of consumerism, we're here to identify four free agents -- two pitchers and two position players -- who could qualify as bargains. The only ground rule is the player must not have ranked among our top 50 free agents. Everyone else is fair game and that allows us to cast a wide net. More than 140 players are free agents right now.

Here, listed alphabetically, are our four Black Friday free agents.

After years as a perfectly cromulent back-end starter/swingman type, Alexander turned in an excellent season as a traditional short reliever with the Rangers in 2026. He pitched in every role. He opened five games, saved four games, set up, matched up against lefties, you name it. That said, only 13 times in 75 appearances did Alexander record more than three outs. He was a one-inning guy.

What makes Alexander, 32, stand out is the breadth of his arsenal and his ability to limit exit velocity. He threw five pitches (sinker, four-seamer, cutter, changeup, sweeper) between 18% and 23% of the time this past season, and that's very rare out of the bullpen. Hitters are used to seeing two, maybe three pitchers from a reliever. Alexander instead plays a five-pitch guessing game.

Alexander's four-seamer and sweeper in particular grade out well analytically, and the five-pitch approach makes him exceedingly difficult to square up. He was among the very best in the game at limiting hard contact. The numbers:

Alexander struck out 19.2% of the batters he faced this summer, below the 22.4% reliever average, and that's why he's a bargain rather than a premium free agent. Strikeouts are the best outcome for a pitcher, but they are expensive. The next best thing is weak contact and Alexander gets it, particularly on the ground. His 49.5% ground ball rate was well above the 42.0% reliever average.

The elevator pitch says Alexander has never beaten himself with walks, he will get weak ground balls, and his wide arsenal makes him effective against both lefties and righties. You might not want him as your go-to high-leverage guy or even your second- or third-best late-inning option, but Alexander has a skill set that suggests he can get important outs for a World Series contender.

It is no coincidence that Civale's first three MLB teams were the analytically inclined Guardians, Rays, and Brewers. He's always been a pitch data darling. The results didn't always match the stuff and that was true this year, when Civale got blasted for 16 home runs in only 74 ⅔ innings with the Athletics. That's exactly one home run every 4 ⅔ innings. Quite bad, in other words.

The A's designated Civale for assignment during the All-Star break and sent him to the Cubs in a minor trade soon thereafter. The Cubs used him exclusively in relief, sometimes for as long as four innings, and the results markedly improved both on the surface and under the hood. Here are the numbers:

There was more to Civale's success with the Cubs than the role change. Chicago cut back on his four-seamer and sinker, upped his cutter usage (the Cubs love pitchers who cut their fastball), and more than doubled his splitter usage. It was a pretty straightforward case of "stop throwing your worst pitches and throw your best pitches more." Sometimes it really is that simple.

Now 31, Civale seems to be at the point where a full-time move into the bullpen gives him the best chance to carve out a lengthy second phase to his career. This is the natural order of things. No. 4-5 type starters, which Civale was earlier in his career, move to the bullpen when their stuff slips and their effectiveness wanes. This is how those guys remain employed.

Modern pitching staffs often include a utility pitcher, the guy who can cover three innings one day and pitch a high-leverage inning the next time out. They want a pitcher who isn't locked into one set role and can instead fill several roles. Civale, with his new pitch mix, seems capable of filling that role, which is not sexy but is something teams need to get to the finish line of 162 games.

I understand baseball players and professional athletes are wired differently than us mere mortals, but I'm always amazed to hear about a player playing through a major injury, especially when his performance goes in the tank. That was the case with Laureano this past season. He played through a hip injury that ultimately required season-ending surgery.

"I have no idea why I kept playing," Laureano told The Athletic in September. "I'm such an idiot. Stupid, really. That's some stupid shit right there."

Laureano, 32, played 53 games with the Padres before going on the injured list and was simply dreadful. His mobility, both at the plate and in the field, was clearly diminished, which isn't surprising for a player with a torn hip labrum. Laureano had surgery in early June and the 4-5 month recovery time puts him on track to be ready for the start of spring training.

Laureano has two things going for him. Well, three things when you include his now-repaired hip. First, his contact quality, despite the hip injury, was quite good in his 53 games and right in line with previous years. His 14.3% barrel rate was legitimately excellent and roughly double the MLB average. Laureano was still able to hit the ball hard and in the air.

And second, there is a shortage of quality right-handed hitters in baseball right now. For a variety of reasons, the game is skewing very left-handed at the moment. Here are the percentages of plate appearances taken by left-handed hitters over the last few years:

That 48.7% is the highest since at least 1961. Quality right-handed hitters are in short supply and Laureano, who has always hit lefties well, is one year removed from a .281/.342/.512 line with 24 homers for the Orioles and Padres. You needn't look back far to see the last time he was very productive, and the hip injury is a tangible explanation for his terrible 2026.

As an everyday player, Laureano might be a bit stretched, but if you're looking for a right-handed platoon outfielder and don't want to meet Tyrone Taylor's asking price or swim in the Victor Robles/Myles Straw waters, Laureano's track record and contact quality (and healthy hip) could make him a nifty dice roll. Good health can be a market inefficiency.

Unlike the other three players in this post, Vierling is not an Article XX(B) free agent, meaning he didn't reach the six years of service time needed for free agency. He was non-tendered by the Tigers. Detroit opted to cut Vierling loose rather than pay a projected $3.5 million or so through arbitration in 2027. After a poor season, it was an understandable baseball decision.

Vierling, 30, is versatile enough to cover all three outfield positions well and play the non-shortstop infield positions in a pinch. He's a right-handed hitter who's always hit lefties reasonably well (including 2026), and, frankly, the Tigers played him too much. When healthy, Detroit often treated Vierling as an everyday player, not as a platoon guy.

Here are Vierling's plate appearance splits over the last five years. This is simply too many plate appearances against righties:

Playing Vierling, a career .236/.293/.374 hitter against righties, that much against right-handed hitters set him up to fail. I get it. The Tigers were in contention only two of those five years and they gave Vierling a chance to show he can be more than a platoon guy, but they never adjusted his role. Even this year, he played just about every day when healthy.

Multiple injuries, including shoulder and oblique strains in 2025 and a groin strain in 2026, landed Vierling on the injured list for 202 total days over the last two years. Availability is the best ability and Vierling didn't have it the last two years. That surely factored into the decision to non-tender him. All indications are that Vierling will be ready to go for spring training, however.

There is a useful player here. Vierling's ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) has been above average most of his career, he can hit lefties, and he's a versatile defender who can give you coverage at most positions. Sometimes less is more. Vierling has the skill set of a good righty platoon bat who can occupy a bench spot for a contender.
